Example: a shopper notices an ad, understands a warranty claim, connects it with the brand and recalls it during comparison. ## Module 3: Social and Cultural Environment — 20% Q7. Explain culture, subculture, cultural change and cross-cultural marketing. Introduction What we eat, wear, celebrate and value is largely shaped by the society we grow up in. According to Schiffman, culture is the sum total of learned beliefs, values, customs, knowledge, art and behaviour shared by members of a society and passed from one generation to the next. 1. Characteristics of Culture 1. Learned: acquired from family, school and society – not inborn. 2. Shared: common to members of a group. 3. Transmitted: passed from generation to generation. 4. Dynamic: changes over time (e.g., acceptance of online shopping). 5. Satisfies needs: provides guidelines for eating, dressing and behaving. 6. Invisible hand: influences us without our noticing. 7. Adaptive and integrated: its elements fit together into a whole. 2. Elements of Culture Values, norms, customs, rituals, symbols, language and religion. 3. Relevance to Marketing Decisions 1. Product: McDonald's in India offers the McAloo Tikki, vegetarian options and no beef products. 2. Communication: ads use regional languages, festivals and family themes. 3. Colours and symbols: white for mourning in some cultures; red for weddings in India. 4. Timing: sales during Diwali, Durga Puja, Eid and Christmas. 5. Packaging and pricing: festival gift packs, small sachets. 6. Avoiding offence: respecting religious and cultural sensitivities. Comparison Table | Marketing decision | Cultural influence | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Product | Food habits, religion | McAloo Tikki | | Promotion | Language, festivals | Regional-language Diwali ads | | Packaging | Colours, gifting customs | Festive gift boxes | | Timing | Festival calendar | Durga Puja sales | Example: Cadbury links its chocolates with Indian festivals and family celebrations through the "Kuch meetha ho jaaye" theme. Values, change and cross-cultural influence: Cultural values guide what a society considers desirable. Changes in work, family roles and environmental concerns can change demand. Explain economic, demographic and social-class influences. Introduction Every society has people at different levels of wealth and status. A social class is a group of people with similar status, values, lifestyles and behaviour. 1. Determinants of Social Class Income, occupation, education, wealth, family background and place of residence. 2. Features of Social Class 1. Hierarchical: upper, middle and lower. 2. Relatively permanent: but mobility (upward or downward) is possible. 3. Multi-dimensional: not based on income alone. 4. Similar consumption patterns among members. 3. Influence on Buying Behaviour 1. Upper class: luxury and premium brands, exclusivity, foreign travel, quality over price. 2. Middle class: value for money, branded but affordable products, spending on education, EMIs. 3. Lower class: price-sensitive, essentials, local brands, small packs, immediate needs. 4. Marketing Uses 1. Segmentation by class. 2. Product and price levels (economy vs premium variants). 3. Store choice and media selection. 4. Advertising themes. Explain reference groups, personal influence and opinion leadership. Introduction People often look to others before deciding what to buy or wear. A reference group is any person or group that serves as a point of comparison or reference for an individual in forming attitudes, values or behaviour. 1. Types of Reference Groups 1. Primary group: small, frequent face-to-face contact – family, close friends. 2. Secondary group: less frequent, more formal contact – clubs, professional bodies. 3. Formal group: defined structure and rules – college committee, company. 4. Informal group: loose, friendship-based – friends circle, gym buddies. 5. Membership group: the person belongs to it – classmates. 6. Aspirational group: the person wants to belong to it – cricket stars, successful entrepreneurs. 7. Dissociative group: the person avoids being associated with it. 8. Virtual / online group: Instagram influencers, online communities. 2. Types of Reference Group Influence 1. Informational influence: seeking expert advice (asking a tech-savvy friend about laptops). 2. Utilitarian (normative) influence: complying to gain approval or avoid rejection (wearing branded shoes because friends do). 3. Value-expressive influence: buying to express a desired self-image (using a brand linked with an admired celebrity). 3. Factors Affecting the Degree of Influence 1. Visibility of the product (clothes and cars are more influenced). 2. Consumer's own experience and knowledge. 3. Credibility and power of the group. 4. Consumer's need for conformity. 4. Marketing Applications Celebrity endorsements, expert endorsements (doctors for toothpaste), common-person testimonials, influencer marketing and brand communities. Personal influence and opinion leadership: Advice, word of mouth and recommendations affect choices. An opinion leader is influential in a particular product category because of experience, credibility or expertise. Influence can be informational (useful evidence), normative (approval) or value-expressive (identity). A knowledgeable friend's phone recommendation is an example. Q10. Explain family roles, structure, life cycle and changing purchase decisions. Introduction Many purchases are made for or by the family. A family is two or more persons related by blood, marriage or adoption who live together. Nuclear family: parents and children. 2. Joint / extended family: grandparents, parents, uncles and children together (common in India). 3. Single-parent families and single-person households: growing in cities. 2. Functions of the Family 1. Economic well-being. 2. Emotional support. 3. A suitable family lifestyle. 4. Consumer socialisation of children. 3. Buying Roles Within the Family 1. Initiator: suggests the idea (child wants a smart TV). 2. Influencer: gives advice (elder sibling recommends a brand). 3. Decider: makes the final decision (father or mother). 4. Buyer: actually purchases (father orders online). 5. User: uses the product (whole family). 6. Gatekeeper: controls the flow of information (mother filters which offers are considered). 4. Types of Husband–Wife Decisions 1. Husband-dominated: e.g., car, insurance (traditionally). 2. Wife-dominated: e.g., kitchen items, groceries, children's clothing. 3. Joint (syncratic): house, holidays, furniture. 4. Autonomic: either spouse decides independently – personal items. Comparison Table | Role | Who (TV purchase) | | --- | --- | | Initiator | Child | | Influencer | Elder sibling | | Decider | Parents | | Buyer | Father | | User | Whole family | | Gatekeeper | Mother | Family life cycle and change: Typical stages include single adults, newly formed households, households with children, older households and solitary survivors; actual families follow varied paths. Joint/nuclear structures, dual incomes, children's influence and changing gender roles affect who initiates, influences, decides, buys and uses a product. ## Module 4: Motivation, Personality, Perception and Learning — 20%; 12 hours Q11. Explain needs, goals, motivation and motive arousal. Introduction Every purchase begins with a reason to buy. According to Schiffman, motivation is the driving force within individuals that impels them to action. It is produced by a state of tension caused by an unfulfilled need; people buy products to reduce this tension. 1. The Motivation Process 1. An unfulfilled need creates tension. 2. Tension produces a drive to act. 3. The drive leads to behaviour (searching and buying). 4. Behaviour achieves a goal, which fulfils the need and reduces tension. 5. Learning and cognitive processes shape which behaviour and goal are chosen. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Unfulfilled needs,
wants and desires"] --> B["Tension"] --> C["Drive"] --> D["Behaviour
(buying)"] --> E["Goal or need
fulfilment"] --> F["Tension
reduction"] G["Learning"] --> A H["Cognitive processes"] --> G D --> H ``` 2. Types of Needs 1. Innate (primary / biogenic) needs: physiological – food, water, shelter, clothing. 2. Acquired (secondary / psychogenic) needs: learned from culture and environment – esteem, prestige, affection, power. 3. Goals Goals are the sought-after results of motivated behaviour. 1. Generic goal: a general category that satisfies a need ("I want a phone"). 2. Product-specific goal: a specific brand or product ("I want an iPhone 17"). 3. Positive goals: objects people approach (healthy food). 4. Negative goals: objects people avoid (avoiding sugar). 4. Rational vs Emotional Motives 1. Rational motives: objective criteria – price, size, fuel efficiency. 2. Emotional motives: subjective criteria – pride, love, fear, status. 5. Features of Needs and Goals 1. Needs are never fully satisfied. 2. New needs arise when old ones are met. 3. Success and failure change the level of aspiration. 4. One goal may satisfy many needs. 5. Substitute goals are used when the preferred goal is blocked. Motive arousal: Needs may be activated physiologically (hunger), emotionally (desire for belonging), cognitively (thinking about a future goal), or environmentally (seeing an advertisement). Maslow's hierarchy of needs Q13. Explain personality, its determinants, development and measurement. Introduction Two consumers with the same income may buy very different brands because they are different kinds of people. According to Schiffman, personality is the set of inner psychological characteristics that both determine and reflect how a person responds to their environment. 1. Nature of Personality 1. Reflects individual differences: no two people are exactly alike, though groups may share traits. 2. Consistent and enduring: relatively stable over time. 3. Can change: due to major life events or gradual maturity. 2. Determinants of Personality 1. Heredity (biological): inherited traits such as physique, temperament and intelligence. 2. Environment: the surroundings in which a person grows up. 3. Family: parents' behaviour, upbringing, birth order and family values. 4. Culture: values and norms of society (individualism vs collectivism). 5. Social / reference groups: friends, school and peer groups. 6. Situation: specific circumstances can bring out different traits. 7. Life experiences: success, failure, education and travel. 3. Marketing Relevance Consumers choose brands whose brand personality matches their own – for example, Thums Up = bold and adventurous; Dove = gentle and caring. Comparison Table | Determinant | Type | Example of influence | | --- | --- | --- | | Heredity | Biological | Energetic temperament | | Family | Social | Thrifty habits learned from parents | | Culture | Social | Collectivist values | | Situation | Environmental | Confident at work, shy at parties | Example: An adventurous young man is drawn to Thums Up's "Toofani" image because it matches his bold personality. Development and measurement: Personality develops through interaction between heredity, family, culture, learning, experience and situations. Measurement uses self-report inventories, rating scales, observation, interviews and projective techniques. Responses can be biased; personality does not determine each purchase on its own. How personality is measured: Define the trait being studied, choose an appropriate validated inventory or observation method, collect responses consistently, score them according to the instrument, and interpret them with attention to reliability, validity and the setting. Self-report questionnaires are convenient but can suffer from socially desirable responding; projective interpretations are subjective and should not be treated as definitive. Development reflects continuing interaction between biological dispositions, socialisation and experience, so a trait profile is neither a permanent label nor a complete purchase prediction. Q14. Compare the personality theories in the syllabus. Introduction Psychoanalytic theories explain personality through inner conflicts and unconscious forces. Sigmund Freud founded this approach, and his followers, the Neo-Freudians, modified it by stressing social relationships. 1. Psychoanalytic Theory (Sigmund Freud) 1. Personality results from the interaction of the id, ego and superego. 2. Unconscious needs, especially biological drives, are central to motivation and personality. 3. Personality develops through psychosexual stages in childhood – oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital. 4. Marketing use: symbolism in ads, motivation research, products that satisfy hidden desires. 2. Neo-Freudian Theory Freud's followers believed social relationships, not sexual instincts, are fundamental to personality. 1. Alfred Adler: people strive to overcome feelings of inferiority ("style of life"). 2. Harry Stack Sullivan: people seek significant relationships to reduce anxiety. 3. Karen Horney – CAD model: people are classified as Compliant, Aggressive or Detached. These are illustrative appeals, not reliable predictions of an individual's purchase. Memory aid: CAD = Compliant (towards), Aggressive (against), Detached (away). Other syllabus theories: Self-concept links purchases to actual self, ideal self, social self and ideal social self. Trait theory describes relatively enduring measurable characteristics, such as innovativeness. Humanistic theory emphasises growth and self-actualisation. Social-cognitive theory explains reciprocal influence between person, behaviour and environment, including self-efficacy. These complement psychoanalytic and Neo-Freudian explanations. Q15. Explain perception and the stages of the perceptual process. Introduction Consumers are surrounded by thousands of stimuli every day, but they notice and remember only a few. The perceptual process explains how a stimulus is received, noticed, organised, understood and remembered. Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["EXPOSURE
stimulus reaches senses"] --> B["ATTENTION
focus on some stimuli"] --> C["ORGANISATION
arrange into patterns"] --> D["INTERPRETATION
give meaning"] --> E["RETENTION
store in memory"] ``` Stages of the Perceptual Process 1. Exposure: a stimulus comes within range of the senses (seeing a billboard, hearing a jingle). Consumers practise selective exposure – they seek pleasant or useful messages and avoid others (skipping ads). 2. Attention: the consumer focuses mental effort on some stimuli. Attention is drawn by size, colour, contrast, movement, novelty, position, celebrities and personal relevance. 3. Organisation: stimuli are grouped into meaningful wholes using Gestalt principles: - Figure and ground: the product (figure) should stand out from the background. - Grouping: items placed together are seen as related (product + lifestyle). - Closure: people complete incomplete pictures (partial logos, unfinished jingles). 4. Interpretation: giving meaning to stimuli based on experience, expectations, culture and motives; different consumers may interpret the same ad differently. 5. Retention: storing the interpreted information in memory; consumers remember messages consistent with their beliefs (selective retention). Comparison Table | Stage | What happens | Marketing tip | | --- | --- | --- | | Exposure | Stimulus reaches senses | Place ads where the target audience is | | Attention | Consumer focuses | Use colour, contrast, novelty | | Organisation | Grouping into patterns | Use figure–ground, closure | | Interpretation | Meaning given | Keep the message clear | | Retention | Stored in memory | Repeat, use jingles | Example: A bright yellow billboard (attention) showing an incomplete famous logo (closure) makes drivers notice and remember the brand. Memory aid: "Every Apple Orchard Is Ripe" – Exposure, Attention, Organisation, Interpretation, Retention. Meaning and importance: Perception is how consumers select, organise and interpret sensory information. It is subjective and selective, so the same price, package or advertisement may mean different things to different people. Perception shapes attention, brand image, perceived quality, risk and value. Q16. Explain sensory elements, thresholds and barriers to accurate perception. Introduction Perception begins when our senses receive a stimulus. The basic elements of perception explain when consumers notice a stimulus and how much change is needed before they notice a difference. 1. Sensation The immediate response of the sense organs (eyes, ears, nose, mouth, skin) to simple stimuli such as an ad, a package or a sound. Sensory adaptation means getting used to a stimulus so that it is no longer noticed – so marketers change ads regularly. 2. Absolute Threshold The lowest level at which a person can detect a stimulus – the point between "nothing" and "something". Example: the distance at which a driver can just notice a billboard. 3. Differential Threshold / Just Noticeable Difference (JND) The minimum difference between two stimuli that can be detected. 4. Weber's Law The stronger the initial stimulus, the greater the additional change needed for the difference to be noticed. The JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus. $$ K = \frac{\Delta I}{I} $$ (K = constant, ΔI = smallest noticeable change, I = initial intensity) Numerical Example Given: price of a chocolate I = ₹50; JND constant K = 0.10. To find: smallest noticeable price change ΔI. Formula: ΔI = K × I Solution: ΔI = 0.10 × 50 = ₹5 Answer: ₹5. Interpretation: under the illustrative assumption, ₹5 is the estimated just-noticeable change. Real price noticing depends on context; Weber's law is an approximation, not a guaranteed rule for shoppers. 5. Marketing Applications of JND 1. Below the JND: reduce pack size, raise price or update logos gradually (shrinkflation, gradual logo evolution) so negative changes are not noticed. 2. Above the JND: make improvements, discounts and "20% extra" offers large enough to be noticed. Comparison Table | Element | Meaning | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Sensation | Immediate sensory response | Hearing a jingle | | Absolute threshold | Minimum detectable level | Distance to notice a billboard | | JND | Minimum noticeable difference | ₹5 on a ₹50 chocolate | | Weber's law | JND is a constant proportion | Bigger price needs bigger change | Sensory dynamics and barriers: Sight, sound, smell, taste and touch influence product experience. Barriers include selective attention, selective distortion, selective retention, stereotypes, halo effects, information overload and perceptual defence. Example: attractive packaging may create an unjustified impression of superior product quality. Sensory dynamics: Colour and shape affect visual impressions; music and sound affect atmosphere; scent can cue memories; texture affects perceived quality; taste affects food evaluation. Match sensory cues to the intended positioning and test responses instead of assuming one universal effect. Perceptual barriers: Selective attention filters out much information; distortion interprets a message through existing beliefs; selective retention favours some information in memory; perceptual defence avoids threatening messages; stereotyping applies group assumptions; the halo effect generalises one impression to other attributes. Reduce misunderstanding through clear claims, accessible design, credible evidence and consistent product experience. Q17. How does perception affect consumer decision-making? Explain perception of products and brands, price, risk and advertising. Introduction Consumers decide on the basis of what they perceive, not on objective facts. Perception shapes how they judge products and brands, prices, risks and advertisements, and therefore what they finally buy. 1. Perception of Products and Brands 1. Consumers use intrinsic cues (size, colour, taste, ingredients) and extrinsic cues (price, brand name, packaging, store image, country of origin). 2. Positioning creates a distinct perception (Volvo = safety; Amul = the taste of India). 3. Brand image and perceived quality drive preference. 2. Perception of Price 1. Perceived value: what consumers believe they get for what they pay. 2. Reference price: the price used for comparison ("MRP ₹999, now ₹699"). 3. Price–quality relationship: a higher price is often seen as higher quality, especially when few other cues exist. 4. Psychological (odd) pricing: ₹499 feels much cheaper than ₹500. 5. Perceived fairness: sudden price hikes are seen as unfair. 3. Perception of Risk Perceived risk is the uncertainty consumers feel when they cannot predict the results of a purchase. 1. Functional risk: the product may not work. 2. Financial risk: money may be wasted. 3. Physical risk: harm to health or safety. 4. Social risk: embarrassment before others. 5. Psychological risk: damage to self-image. 6. Time risk: time lost if the product fails. How consumers reduce risk: seek information and reviews, stay brand loyal, buy well-known brands, rely on store image, buy the most expensive model, buy small quantities, look for warranties, return policies and free trials. How marketers reduce risk: guarantees, free samples, money-back offers, testimonials, certifications (ISI, FSSAI) and demonstrations. 4. Perception and Advertising 1. Ads must first gain exposure and attention, then be interpreted correctly. 2. Key factors: source credibility, message clarity, repetition, music, celebrities, humour, emotional appeals. 3. Perception of the ad affects attitude towards the ad and the brand, and finally purchase. 4. Misleading ads damage trust once detected. Comparison Table (types of perceived risk) | Type of risk | Meaning | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Functional | Product may not work | New phone brand may fail | | Financial | Money wasted | Expensive laptop | | Physical | Harm to health | New medicine | | Social | Embarrassment | Unfashionable clothes | | Psychological | Damage to self-image | Wrong luxury brand | | Time | Time lost | Returning a faulty product | Example: An online seller offers a 10-day free return policy to reduce the financial and functional risk of buying shoes without trying them on. Perceptual mapping is a visual technique that shows how consumers perceive competing brands on two or more important attributes. Understand how consumers see your brand versus competitors. 2. Identify market gaps for new products (an affordable sporty car). 3. Plan repositioning if the brand is in the wrong place. 4. Track changes in perception over time. Advantages: - Simple visual view of competition. - Reveals new product opportunities. Limitations: - Based on perceptions, which may change. - Two axes simplify reality.
