Consumer imagery and subliminal perception: Consumer imagery is the mental picture of a brand, product, store or service, formed by experience and marketing cues. Subliminal perception concerns stimuli below conscious awareness; do not claim it reliably controls purchases. A perceptual map uses consumers' perceived attributes, not necessarily objective product measurements. Types of consumer imagery: Product/brand image concerns associated qualities and symbolic meanings; store image concerns assortment, service and atmosphere; service image draws on staff, processes and physical cues; price–quality imagery concerns what a price suggests about quality; corporate image concerns the organisation's reputation. Images can differ from objective performance, so research the audience's actual associations. Subliminal versus ordinary persuasion: Subliminal stimuli are presented below conscious awareness; subtle but consciously detectable design is not automatically subliminal. Do not infer reliable buying control from laboratory effects or popular claims. Consumer choice also depends on existing needs, attention, context and alternatives. Q19. Explain learning and classical conditioning with marketing examples. Introduction Classical conditioning, developed by Ivan Pavlov, is learning by association. A neutral stimulus, repeatedly paired with a stimulus that naturally produces a response, starts producing a similar response on its own. It is a form of stimulus–response learning. 1. Pavlov's Experiment | Stage | Stimulus | Response | | --- | --- | --- | | Before | Food (UCS)
Bell (neutral) | Salivation (UCR)
No response | | During (repeated pairing) | Bell (CS) + Food (UCS) | Salivation (UCR) | | After | Bell (CS) alone | Salivation (CR) | 1. Unconditioned stimulus (UCS): naturally causes a response (food). 2. Unconditioned response (UCR): the natural response (salivation). 3. Conditioned stimulus (CS): a neutral stimulus that becomes linked (bell). 4. Conditioned response (CR): the learned response to the CS (salivation to the bell). 2. Key Concepts and Marketing Applications 1. Repetition: strengthens the association (repeated ads, jingles). Too much repetition causes advertising wear-out, so ads are varied (cosmetic or substantive variation). 2. Stimulus generalisation: responding in the same way to similar stimuli. - Product line / form extension: Dettol soap and handwash benefit from Dettol antiseptic. - Family branding: the Tata name across many products. - Licensing: cartoon characters on products. - Look-alike packaging by private labels. 3. Stimulus discrimination: telling similar stimuli apart – the basis of positioning and differentiation ("accept no substitutes", unique packaging). Comparison Table | Concept | Meaning | Marketing example | | --- | --- | --- | | Repetition | Repeated pairing strengthens learning | Repeated jingles | | Stimulus generalisation | Same response to similar stimuli | Dettol handwash, family branding | | Stimulus discrimination | Different responses to similar stimuli | Unique packaging, positioning | Example: A soft-drink brand (CS) is shown repeatedly with happy friends and festive music (UCS), so consumers feel cheerful (CR) on seeing the brand alone. Learning essentials: Learning is a relatively lasting change in knowledge or behaviour from experience. Motives, cues, responses and reinforcement matter. Classical conditioning links stimuli; operant conditioning links behaviour to consequences. A familiar jingle associated with pleasant feelings illustrates the former; loyalty points rewarding repeat purchase illustrate the latter. Q20. Compare the remaining behavioural and cognitive learning theories. Definition: Behavioural learning theories explain learning as a response to external stimuli and rewards, while cognitive learning theories explain learning as the result of mental processes such as thinking and problem-solving. Key points: 1. Behavioural theories treat the consumer as passive; cognitive theories treat the consumer as an active problem-solver. 2. Behavioural learning suits low-involvement purchases; cognitive learning suits high-involvement purchases. 3. Behavioural tools are jingles, repetition and rewards; cognitive tools are detailed information, comparisons and demos. | Basis | Behavioural learning | Cognitive learning | | --- | --- | --- | | View of consumer | Passive, responds to stimuli | Active problem-solver | | Focus | Observable behaviour (stimulus–response) | Mental processes (thinking, memory) | | How learning happens | Association, reinforcement, repetition | Information processing, reasoning, insight | | Theories | Classical, operant, trial-and-error, social learning | Social cognitive, cognitive behavioural, constructivism | | Best for | Low-involvement purchases | High-involvement purchases | | Marketing tools | Jingles, repetition, rewards | Detailed information, comparisons, demos | Example: A biscuit brand relies on catchy jingles (behavioural), while a laptop brand provides detailed specification comparisons (cognitive). Compact syllabus theory notes: | Theory | Main idea | Consumer example | | --- | --- | --- | | Cognitive associative / memory-based learning | Learn and remember relationships between cues and outcomes | Recognise a brand associated with reliable quality | | Trial-and-error learning | Repeated attempts and their consequences shape later choices | Try brands and repeat the satisfactory one | | Operant / instrumental conditioning | Reinforcement increases a response; unrewarded responses may weaken | Reward points encourage repeat buying | | Social learning | Attention, retention, reproduction and motivation support learning from models | Learn product use from a demonstration | | Social cognitive | Person, behaviour and environment interact; self-efficacy matters | A tutorial builds confidence in using an appliance | | Cognitive behavioural | Thoughts, feelings and behaviour influence one another | Reconsider an impulse purchase by questioning a belief | | Constructivism | Build understanding by relating new experience to existing knowledge | Learn through trials, comparisons and discussion | The syllabus groups some overlapping approaches together. Association, trial-and-error and observational learning are related but should not be treated as identical. ## Module 5: Consumer Decision Making — 20% Q21. Explain the buying process, information search, decision rules and post-purchase evaluation. Introduction Buying is not a single act; it is a process that starts before the purchase and continues after it. The five-stage consumer decision-making process explains the steps a consumer goes through – from recognising a need to evaluating the product after use. Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart TD A["1. Problem recognition
need is felt"] --> B["2. Information search
internal and external"] B --> C["3. Evaluation of alternatives
compare brands on evaluative criteria"] C --> D["4. Purchase decision
brand, store, time, quantity, payment"] D --> E["5. Post-purchase evaluation
satisfaction or dissonance"] E -. "feedback: repurchase / complaint / word of mouth" .-> A ``` 1. Problem (Need) Recognition 1. The consumer notices a difference between the actual state and the desired state. 2. It is triggered by internal stimuli (hunger, a slow phone) or external stimuli (ads, friends' new products, festival offers). 3. Actual-state type: a product stops working. Desired-state type: desire for something new or better. 2. Information Search 1. Internal search (memory) and external search (personal, commercial, public and experiential sources). 2. Result: the evoked (consideration) set of brands. 3. Evaluation of Alternatives 1. Brands in the evoked set are compared using evaluative criteria (price, features, brand, reviews). 2. Consumers use decision rules – compensatory and non-compensatory. 4. Purchase Decision (Purchase Selection) 1. The consumer forms a purchase intention and decides brand, store, quantity, timing and payment method. 2. Intention can change because of attitudes of others (a friend's negative opinion) and unexpected situational factors (job loss, out-of-stock, price rise). 3. Types of purchase: trial purchase, repeat purchase, long-term commitment. 5. Post-Purchase Evaluation 1. The consumer compares performance with expectations – dissatisfied, satisfied or delighted. 2. Post-purchase (cognitive) dissonance: doubt after a major purchase ("Did I make the right choice?"). 3. Consumers reduce dissonance by seeking positive reviews, avoiding negative information or returning the product. 4. Marketers' role: follow-up calls, thank-you messages, warranties, easy returns, reassurance ads, customer support. 5. Outcomes: repeat purchase and loyalty, positive or negative word of mouth, complaints, product disposal. Comparison Table | Stage | Key question | Marketer's action | | --- | --- | --- | | Problem recognition | "Do I need something?" | Ads that trigger needs | | Information search | "What are my options?" | Be visible online and in stores | | Evaluation | "Which is best?" | Highlight key attributes | | Purchase | "Where, when, how?" | Availability, easy payment | | Post-purchase | "Was it right?" | Follow-up, warranties | Example: Riya's old phone becomes slow (problem recognition); she reads reviews (search), compares three models (evaluation), buys one on a festival sale (purchase) and posts a positive review (post-purchase). Memory aid: "Please Investigate Each Product Properly" – Problem recognition, Information search, Evaluation, Purchase, Post-purchase. Search and evaluation: Internal search retrieves memory; external search uses personal, commercial, public and experiential sources. Evaluative criteria include price, quality, features and service. A compensatory rule allows strength on one attribute to offset weakness on another; non-compensatory rules include minimum cut-offs, choosing by the most important attribute and elimination by aspects. Post-purchase dissonance: Doubt after choosing, especially for an expensive purchase. Honest information, reliable performance, clear support and appropriate reassurance can reduce it. Q22. What is a consumer decision? Explain the types of consumer decisions. Introduction Consumers make many buying decisions every day, from buying milk to buying a car, but they do not put the same effort into each. According to Schiffman, a consumer decision is the selection of an option from two or more alternatives. If there is no choice, there is no decision. 1. Levels of Consumer Decision Making (by effort) 1. Extensive problem solving: high effort, much information search and evaluation; used for first-time, expensive, high-risk purchases with no set criteria. Example: first car, laptop, house. 2. Limited problem solving: moderate effort; criteria are known but brands are new. Example: a new shampoo brand, a new phone model. 3. Routinised response (habitual) behaviour: very little or no effort; frequent, low-cost, familiar products. Example: toothpaste, milk, bread. 2. Types of Buying Behaviour (Assael) – by involvement and brand differences 1. Complex buying behaviour: high involvement, significant brand differences (laptop, car). 2. Dissonance-reducing behaviour: high involvement, few brand differences (carpet, cement). 3. Variety-seeking behaviour: low involvement, significant brand differences (biscuits, snacks). 4. Habitual buying behaviour: low involvement, few brand differences (salt, sugar). | | High involvement | Low involvement | | --- | --- | --- | | Significant brand differences | Complex buying (laptop, car) | Variety-seeking (biscuits, snacks) | | Few brand differences | Dissonance-reducing (carpet, cement) | Habitual (salt, sugar) | 3. Other Classifications 1. Impulse buying: unplanned and emotional. 2. Planned buying. 3. Individual vs joint (family) decisions. 4. Personal vs organisational decisions. Comparison Table (levels of decision making) | Type | Effort and search | When used | Example | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Extensive | High | First-time, costly, risky | First car | | Limited | Moderate | Known criteria, new brands | New shampoo brand | | Routinised | Very little | Frequent, cheap, familiar | Toothpaste | Example: A student spends weeks comparing laptops (extensive), a few minutes choosing a new shampoo (limited) and no time picking her usual toothpaste (routinised). Memory aid: "E-L-R" = Extensive, Limited, Routine – effort goes from high to low. Q23. Explain the buying pattern of consumers in the new digital era. Introduction Smartphones, the internet and digital payments have transformed shopping. In the digital era, consumers search, evaluate, buy and share their experiences very differently from the past, and they have far more information and choice. 1. Key Features of Digital-Era Buying 1. Online research before buying: comparison websites, specifications, prices and YouTube reviews. 2. Zero Moment of Truth (ZMOT): a term popularised by Google for the moment consumers research online before visiting a store or deciding. 3. Reviews and ratings: strongly influence choice; user-generated content is trusted more than ads. 4. Omnichannel shopping: moving between online and offline – ROPO (research online, purchase offline) and showrooming (see in store, buy online). 5. Mobile commerce and digital payments: UPI, wallets, buy-now-pay-later and one-click buying. 6. Social commerce and influencers: buying through Instagram, YouTube and WhatsApp. 7. Personalisation and AI recommendations: "customers who bought this also bought…". 8. Quick commerce and convenience: groceries delivered in minutes; subscriptions. 9. Empowered consumers: easy price comparison and public complaints on social media. 10. Post-purchase sharing: reviews and unboxing videos influence others. 2. Challenges 1. Information overload. 2. Fake reviews. 3. Privacy concerns. 4. Online fraud. 5. Impulse buying due to easy payments. Comparison Table | Stage | Traditional | Digital era | | --- | --- | --- | | Problem recognition | Ads, needs | Targeted online ads, social media, notifications | | Information search | Friends, salespeople, print ads | Search engines, reviews, videos, comparison sites | | Evaluation | Store visits | Online filters, ratings, specification comparison | | Purchase | Physical store, cash | E-commerce, apps, UPI, EMI, doorstep delivery | | Post-purchase | Word of mouth to a few people | Online reviews reach thousands; easy returns | Example: A shopper sees an Instagram ad for sneakers, checks reviews on YouTube, compares prices on two apps, pays by UPI and later posts an unboxing video. Q24. Explain the four views of consumer decision making. Introduction Different experts see the consumer differently – as a perfect calculator, an easy target, a thinker or an emotional being. Schiffman describes four "models of man" that explain how and why consumers make decisions. 1. Economic Man 1. The consumer is fully rational: knows all alternatives, ranks them correctly by benefits and costs, and chooses the best (utility-maximising) option. 2. Based on classical economic theory. 3. Criticism: unrealistic – consumers rarely have complete information, time or perfect reasoning; they are limited by habits, values and emotions (bounded rationality – they "satisfice" rather than maximise). 2. Passive Man 1. The consumer is submissive to the marketer's promotions – an impulsive, irrational buyer easily persuaded by advertising and salespeople. 2. Basis of traditional selling techniques (AIDA: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action). 3. Criticism: ignores that consumers actively seek information and can resist persuasion. 3. Cognitive Man 1. The consumer is a thinking problem-solver who actively seeks and processes information. 2. Uses heuristics (decision rules) to cope with information overload and stops searching when a satisfactory option is found. 3. Lies midway between the economic and passive views. 4. Emotional Man 1. Decisions are based on feelings, moods and emotions (love, fear, joy, pride) rather than careful search. 2. Often impulsive; common for gifts, luxury items, fashion and comfort food. 3. Mood affects what is noticed, remembered and bought (a pleasant store atmosphere encourages buying). 4. Marketing use: emotional advertising, music, festive themes, store ambience. Comparison Table | View | Consumer is | Information use | Example | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Economic man | Perfectly rational | Complete | Comparing every loan offer for the lowest interest | | Passive man | Easily influenced | Little | Buying because a salesperson persuaded | | Cognitive man | Thinking problem-solver | Enough to decide | Reading reviews before buying a laptop | | Emotional man | Feeling-driven | Little | Buying a gift on impulse for a loved one | Memory aid: "EPCE" – Economic, Passive, Cognitive, Emotional ("Every Person Chooses Emotionally sometimes"). Q25. Explain the Nicosia model of consumer decision making with a diagram. Introduction The Nicosia model (Francesco Nicosia, 1966) focuses on the relationship between the firm and its potential consumer. The firm communicates with the consumer through marketing messages, and the consumer responds through purchase behaviour – the two influence each other in a circular flow. The model has four fields. Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart TD F1["FIELD 1: Source of message → consumer's attitude
Sub-field 1: firm's attributes → message (advertising)
Sub-field 2: consumer's predisposition → exposure → ATTITUDE"] F2["FIELD 2: Search and evaluation (pre-action field)
search and evaluation of alternatives → MOTIVATION"] F3["FIELD 3: The act of purchase
decision → PURCHASE behaviour"] F4["FIELD 4: Feedback
consumption / storage → EXPERIENCE
feedback to the firm (sales data) and the consumer"] F1 -- attitude --> F2 F2 -- motivation --> F3 F3 -- purchase --> F4 F4 -. feedback .-> F1 ``` 1. Field 1 – Consumer Attitude Based on the Firm's Message 1. Sub-field 1: the firm's attributes and marketing environment produce a message (ad, product information). 2. Sub-field 2: the consumer's attributes (personality, experience, predispositions) interpret the message. 3. Output: an attitude towards the product. 2. Field 2 – Search and Evaluation 1. The consumer searches for information and evaluates the brand against alternatives. 2. Output: motivation to buy (or not). 3. Field 3 – Act of Purchase 1. Motivation turns into a decision and the actual purchase from a particular store. 4. Field 4 – Feedback 1. After consumption, the consumer's experience affects future attitudes and predispositions. 2. The firm receives sales results as feedback and adjusts its marketing. Advantages (Merits): - Shows consumer behaviour as a process, not a single act. - Highlights two-way communication between firm and consumer. - Useful for planning advertising and obtaining feedback. Limitations: - Variables are not clearly defined or measured. - Assumes the consumer has no prior attitude (starts with the firm's message). - Focuses mainly on new products; difficult to test empirically. Comparison Table | Field | Activity | Output | | --- | --- | --- | | Field 1 | Firm's message meets consumer's predisposition | Attitude | | Field 2 | Search and evaluation | Motivation | | Field 3 | Decision and buying | Purchase | | Field 4 | Consumption and feedback | Experience / feedback | Example: A new electric-scooter brand advertises (Field 1); a consumer compares it with rivals (Field 2), buys it (Field 3), and her experience plus the firm's sales data shape future attitudes and ads (Field 4). Memory aid: "Attitude → Motivation → Purchase → Feedback" – the output of each field in order. ## Module 6: Communication, Models and Consumer Rights — 20% Q26. Explain the marketing communication process and types of communication. Introduction Even the best product will not sell if consumers do not know about it. Marketing communication is the process by which a firm informs, persuades and reminds consumers about its products and brands. It follows the basic communication model (based on Schramm and Shannon–Weaver). Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart LR S["SENDER
(firm)"] --> EN["ENCODING"] --> M["MESSAGE"] --> C["CHANNEL
(media)"] --> D["DECODING"] --> R["RECEIVER
(consumer)"] R --> RS["RESPONSE"] RS -. FEEDBACK .-> S N["NOISE
(clutter, distraction)"] -.-> C ``` Elements of the Communication Process 1. Sender (source): the organisation or person sending the message – brand, celebrity endorser, salesperson. 2. Encoding: turning ideas into words, images and symbols – writing an ad script, designing visuals. 3. Message: the content communicated – "Strong teeth, fresh breath". 4. Channel (media): the path the message travels – TV, YouTube, Instagram, newspaper, salesperson. 5. Decoding: the receiver interprets the message – the consumer understands the benefit. 6. Receiver: the target audience – young adults, parents. 7. Response: reaction after receiving the message – visiting a website, buying. 8. Feedback: response returned to the sender – sales, likes, comments, surveys. 9. Noise: anything that distorts or interrupts communication – ad clutter, poor signal, distractions. Requirements for Effective Communication 1. A credible source. 2. A clear message. 3. The right channel. 4. Understanding of the audience, so that encoding matches decoding. 5. Reducing noise. Comparison Table | Element | Example (toothpaste ad) | | --- | --- | | Sender | Toothpaste brand | | Encoding | Ad script with a dentist | | Message | "Strong teeth, fresh breath" | | Channel | TV and YouTube | | Receiver | Parents | | Feedback | Sales, comments | | Noise | Too many ads in the break | Example: A toothpaste brand uses a dentist (credible source) on TV (channel) to tell parents (receivers) that it prevents cavities; rising sales are the feedback. Memory aid: "Some Elephants Make Children Dance Rather Fast" – Sender, Encoding, Message, Channel, Decoding, Receiver, Feedback (+ Noise). Communication systems: Interpersonal communication is person-to-person and allows immediate feedback; impersonal communication reaches audiences through media; persuasive communication aims to change beliefs, attitudes or behaviour and may use either channel. Source credibility, clear claims, audience relevance and feedback affect success. Q27. Explain and compare the Black Box and Economic models. Introduction Marketers can see what they offer consumers and what consumers finally buy, but not what happens inside the consumer's mind. The Black Box model (stimulus–response model, popularised by Kotler) shows how marketing and environmental stimuli enter the consumer's mind – the "black box" – and produce buyer responses. Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph ST["STIMULI"] S1["Marketing:
Product, Price, Place, Promotion"] S2["Environmental:
Economic, Technological,
Political, Cultural"] end subgraph BB["BUYER'S BLACK BOX"] B1["Buyer characteristics
(cultural, social, personal, psychological)"] B2["Buyer decision process
(problem recognition → post-purchase)"] end subgraph RE["RESPONSES"] R1["Product choice · Brand choice
Dealer choice · Purchase timing
Purchase amount"] end ST --> BB --> RE ``` Components of the Model 1. Stimuli: marketing stimuli (the 4Ps, controlled by the firm) and environmental stimuli (economic, technological, political and cultural forces). 2. Black box: the consumer's mind – buyer characteristics (how stimuli are perceived) and the buyer decision process – hidden from marketers. 3. Responses: observable outputs – product, brand and dealer choice, purchase timing and amount. Advantages: - Simple and easy to understand. - Helps marketers link the 4Ps to buyer responses. Limitations: - Does not explain the internal processes in detail. - Treats the consumer's mind as unknown. Comparison Table | Part | Contents | Visible to marketer? | | --- | --- | --- | | Stimuli | 4Ps, environment | Yes | | Black box | Buyer characteristics, decision process | No | | Responses | Product, brand, dealer, timing, amount | Yes | Example: A phone company cuts its price and runs a festive ad (stimuli); it cannot see buyers' thoughts, but rising sales of one model (response) show how buyers reacted. Economic model: Buyers are assumed to compare alternatives rationally and seek maximum utility within a budget. Price, income and substitute products affect demand. Its strength is explaining economic trade-offs; its limitation is neglecting incomplete information, emotion, habits and social influences. Q28. Explain the Howard model and the Howard–Sheth model of buyer behaviour. Introduction The Howard model (John Howard, 1963) was an early model that viewed buying as a learning process: a consumer moves from extensive problem solving to limited problem solving and then to routinised response behaviour as experience grows. It was later refined into the Howard–Sheth model (John Howard and Jagdish Sheth, 1969), which explains brand choice behaviour over time, especially repeat buying, by integrating social, psychological and marketing influences. Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph IN["INPUTS (stimuli)"] I1["Significative: quality, price, features"] I2["Symbolic: ads, brand image"] I3["Social: family, groups, class"] end subgraph HC["HYPOTHETICAL CONSTRUCTS"] P["Perceptual constructs
sensitivity to information,
perceptual bias, search for information"] L["Learning constructs
motives, choice criteria, brand comprehension,
attitude, confidence, intention, satisfaction"] end subgraph OUT["OUTPUTS"] O["Attention → Brand comprehension →
Attitude → Intention → Purchase"] end IN --> HC --> OUT EX["EXOGENOUS VARIABLES
importance of purchase, personality, social class,
culture, time pressure, financial status, organisation"] -.-> HC ``` Components of the Howard–Sheth Model 1. Inputs (stimuli): - Significative: actual product attributes – quality, price, distinctiveness, availability. - Symbolic: representations by marketers – ads, brand image. - Social: family, reference groups, social class. 2. Perceptual constructs: how information is received and processed – sensitivity to information, perceptual bias (distortion), search for information. 3. Learning constructs: motives, choice criteria, brand comprehension, attitudes, confidence, intention and satisfaction after purchase. 4. Outputs: attention → comprehension → attitude → intention → purchase behaviour (a hierarchy). 5. Exogenous (external) variables: not directly part of the model – importance of the purchase, personality, social class, culture, time pressure, financial status. Three levels of decision making: extensive problem solving, limited problem solving and routinised response behaviour. Advantages: - Comprehensive. - Explains learning and brand loyalty. - Widely tested. Limitations: - Complex. - Variables are hard to measure. - Mainly for individual repeat purchases. Comparison Table | Component | Contents | | --- | --- | | Inputs | Significative, symbolic, social stimuli | | Perceptual constructs | Sensitivity, perceptual bias, search | | Learning constructs | Motives, choice criteria, attitude, confidence, satisfaction | | Outputs | Attention → comprehension → attitude → intention → purchase | | Exogenous variables | Personality, class, culture, time, finances | Example: A first-time coffee buyer searches widely (extensive problem solving); after a few satisfying purchases of one brand, she buys it routinely (routinised response). Q29. Explain the EKB (Engel–Kollat–Blackwell) model with a diagram. Introduction The EKB model (James Engel, David Kollat and Roger Blackwell, 1968), later called the EBM (Engel–Blackwell–Miniard) model, is a comprehensive model built around the decision-making process of an individual consumer. It shows how information is processed and how internal and external variables influence each decision stage. Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart LR I["INPUT
stimuli from marketers
and others (friends, family)"] --> IP["INFORMATION PROCESSING
exposure → attention → comprehension
→ yielding → retention (MEMORY)"] IP --> DP["DECISION PROCESS
need recognition → search → evaluation
→ purchase → outcomes"] V["VARIABLES INFLUENCING THE DECISION
Individual: motives, values, lifestyle
Environmental: culture, groups, family, situation"] --> DP DP -. "feedback to memory and future search" .-> IP ``` Four Sections of the Model 1. Input: information from marketing sources (ads, salespeople) and non-marketing sources (friends, family, reviews). 2. Information processing: exposure → attention → comprehension → acceptance (yielding) → retention in memory. 3. Decision process (central part, five stages): need recognition → information search → alternative evaluation → purchase → outcomes (satisfaction or dissonance). 4. Variables influencing the decision process: - Individual characteristics: motives, values, lifestyle, personality, attitudes. - Social / environmental influences: culture, reference groups, family, social class. - Situational influences: financial situation, time, store environment. Advantages: - Clear, step-by-step decision process. - Widely used in textbooks and marketing planning. - Recognises both internal and external influences. Limitations: - Variables and their relationships are not fully specified. - Complex to test. - Assumes a highly rational, involved consumer. Comparison Table | Section | Contents | | --- | --- | | Input | Marketing and non-marketing stimuli | | Information processing | Exposure, attention, comprehension, yielding, retention | | Decision process | Need recognition → search → evaluation → purchase → outcomes | | Influencing variables | Individual, environmental, situational | Example: A family buying a washing machine sees ads and asks neighbours (input), remembers the key features (processing), compares models and buys one (decision process), influenced by budget and family needs (variables). Q30. Compare Webster–Wind and Sheth's industrial buying models. Introduction Organisations buy differently from individuals – many people take part and formal rules apply. The Webster and Wind model (Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind, 1972) explains organisational (industrial) buying. Buying decisions are made by a buying centre that is influenced by four groups of variables. Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph ENV["ENVIRONMENTAL: economy, technology, laws, culture, suppliers"] subgraph ORG["ORGANISATIONAL: objectives, policies, structure"] subgraph INTP["INTERPERSONAL (buying centre): roles, authority, status"] IND["INDIVIDUAL: age, education,
personality, risk attitude"] end end end ENV --> BD["BUYING DECISIONS"] ``` 1. Environmental Factors Physical, technological, economic, political, legal and cultural forces, and the availability of suppliers. 2. Organisational Factors The firm's goals, purchasing policies, procedures, structure (centralised or decentralised buying), technology and people. 3. Interpersonal Factors – the Buying Centre All individuals who take part in the buying decision: 1. Initiator: recognises the need – IT staff report slow computers. 2. Users: will use the product – employees. 3. Influencers: help define specifications – IT manager. 4. Buyers: formal authority to select suppliers and negotiate – purchase manager. 5. Deciders: final authority to approve – finance head or director. 6. Gatekeepers: control the flow of information – secretary, purchase assistant. 4. Individual Factors Each participant's age, education, job position, personality, motives, attitude to risk and professional goals. Advantages: - Comprehensive view of organisational buying. - Identifies all influences. - Useful for business-to-business (B2B) marketing. Limitations: - Descriptive rather than predictive. - Does not show the decision steps in detail. Comparison Table | Level | Factors | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Environmental | Economy, technology, laws | New data-protection rules | | Organisational | Policies, structure | Centralised purchasing | | Interpersonal | Buying centre roles | IT manager influences choice | | Individual | Age, motives, risk attitude | Risk-averse purchase manager | Example: When a college buys 100 computers, the IT head (influencer), the principal (decider) and the purchase officer (buyer) are all shaped by budget rules (organisational) and government tender laws (environmental). Memory aid: "EOII" – Environmental, Organisational, Interpersonal, Individual (outer to inner circle). Sheth's industrial buyer behaviour model: Purchasing staff, engineers and users have different expectations shaped by background, information and past satisfaction. Product factors (risk, time pressure, purchase type) and company factors influence autonomous versus joint decisions. Joint decisions can involve problem solving, persuasion, bargaining or politicking; situational factors may change the final choice. Comparison: Webster–Wind organises levels of influence; Sheth emphasises expectations, joint decisions and conflict resolution. Q31. Explain the Consumer Protection Act, 1986: objectives, key definitions and redressal machinery. Syllabus focus: Consumer Protection Act, 1986. Treat this answer as a historical syllabus topic, not a guide to present-day filing rules. The Act aimed to protect consumer interests and provide accessible redress for defective goods, deficient services and unfair trade practices. - Consumer: Broadly, a buyer of goods or hirer/user of services for consideration, subject to statutory inclusions and exclusions. - Defect: A fault in goods, such as their quality, quantity or standard. - Deficiency: A shortcoming in the quality or performance of a service. - Protection councils: Promoted and protected consumer interests. - Redressal structure under the 1986 Act: District Forum → State Commission → National Commission. - Remedies: Removal of defects, replacement, refund, compensation and discontinuance of unfair practices, as applicable. Example: A defective appliance and a refusal to provide an appropriate remedy illustrate why consumer redress is needed. For an exam answer, state the purpose, distinguish defect from deficiency, draw the three-tier structure and explain remedies. The six rights are covered in the next answer. Q32. Explain the rights of consumers. Introduction Consumer rights protect buyers from exploitation and help them make informed choices. The Consumer Protection Act (1986, continued in the 2019 Act) recognises six consumer rights, based on the rights first stated by US President John F. Kennedy in 1962 and expanded by the UN Guidelines for Consumer Protection. The Six Consumer Rights 1. Right to safety: protection against goods and services hazardous to life and property. Example: buying ISI-marked electrical items and FSSAI-approved food. 2. Right to be informed: information about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price. Example: MRP, expiry date and ingredients printed on packs. 3. Right to choose: access to a variety of goods at competitive prices. Example: freedom to choose any brand; no forced bundling. 4. Right to be heard: consumers' interests receive due consideration at appropriate forums. Example: consumer helplines, representation in consumer councils. 5. Right to seek redressal: remedy against unfair trade practices or exploitation. Example: filing a complaint in a Consumer Commission for a defective product. 6. Right to consumer education: the right to acquire knowledge and skills to be an informed consumer. Example: the "Jago Grahak Jago" campaign. Responsibilities of Consumers 1. Be aware of rights and products. 2. Always ask for a bill or cash memo. 3. Check quality marks – ISI, AGMARK, Hallmark, FSSAI. 4. Read labels carefully. 5. File only genuine complaints. 6. Avoid wasteful consumption and form consumer associations. Comparison Table | Right | Protects against | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Safety | Hazardous goods | ISI mark | | Information | Misleading details | MRP, expiry date | | Choice | Monopoly, forced bundling | Many brands available | | Heard | Ignored complaints | Consumer helplines | | Redressal | Exploitation | Consumer Commission | | Education | Ignorance | Jago Grahak Jago | Memory aid: "SICHRE" – Safety, Information, Choice, Heard, Redressal, Education ("Stay Informed, Choose, Hear, Redress, Educate"). ## Additional answers for syllabus depth These expand topics that were too brief in the condensed set. Existing question numbers are unchanged. Q33. What are cross-cultural influences? Why is cross-cultural understanding important? Introduction When companies sell in many countries or regions, they meet consumers with different languages, values and habits. Cross-cultural consumer analysis is the study of similarities and differences between consumers of different cultures or countries, to decide whether to use a standardised or a localised marketing strategy. 1. Areas of Cross-Cultural Difference 1. Language and meanings of words. 2. Values and religion. 3. Food habits. 4. Colours, symbols and gestures. 5. Gift customs and time orientation. 6. Family roles. 7. Level of income and technology. 2. Strategies for Cross-Cultural Marketing 1. Standardisation (global strategy): the same product and message worldwide. Example: Apple iPhone, Coca-Cola logo. 2. Localisation (adaptation): product and message adapted to local culture. Example: McDonald's McAloo Tikki, KFC's vegetarian menu in India. 3. Glocalisation: "think global, act local" – a global brand with local flavours and languages. 3. Importance of Cross-Cultural Understanding 1. Avoids cultural blunders such as wrong translations or offensive symbols. 2. Helps design acceptable products and packaging. 3. Improves communication effectiveness. 4. Builds trust and acceptance in new markets. Advantages of standardisation: lower cost and a consistent global image. Limitations of standardisation: may ignore local needs and cause rejection. Comparison Table | Basis | Standardisation | Localisation | Glocalisation | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Approach | Same everywhere | Adapted to each market | Global core, local touches | | Cost | Low | High | Medium | | Fit with local culture | Low | High | High | | Example | iPhone | McAloo Tikki | Domino's paneer pizzas | Example: A brand name that sounds fine in English may have a negative meaning in another language, so firms test names locally before launch. Q34. Explain the family life cycle and its marketing implications. Introduction A family's needs change as members marry, have children, grow older and retire. The Family Life Cycle (FLC) describes the stages a family passes through over time; each stage has different needs, income and buying patterns. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Bachelor"] --> B["Newly married"] --> C["Full nest I"] --> D["Full nest II"] --> E["Full nest III"] E --> F["Empty nest I"] --> G["Empty nest II"] --> H["Solitary survivor"] ``` Stages of the Family Life Cycle 1. Bachelor stage: young, single, living alone – fashion, gadgets, entertainment, travel. 2. Newly married couple: young, no children – furniture, appliances, holidays, home. 3. Full nest I: youngest child under 6 – baby food, toys, medicines, insurance. 4. Full nest II: youngest child 6 or older – education, tuition, bicycles, larger packs. 5. Full nest III: older couple with dependent grown-up children – higher education, second car, home upgrades. 6. Empty nest I: children have left home, head still working – travel, luxury items, investments. 7. Empty nest II: head retired, lower income – healthcare, pilgrimage, medical insurance. 8. Solitary survivor: one spouse alive – healthcare, care services, companionship. Modern variations: single parents, childless couples, divorced persons, live-in couples and people marrying later. Marketing Implications 1. Target products to each life stage. 2. Time offers to life events (weddings, childbirth, retirement). 3. Design life-stage insurance, banking and housing products. Comparison Table | Stage | Typical purchases | | --- | --- | | Bachelor | Fashion, gadgets | | Newly married | Furniture, appliances | | Full nest I | Baby products, insurance | | Full nest II | Education, larger packs | | Full nest III | Higher education, second car | | Empty nest I | Travel, luxury | | Empty nest II | Healthcare, pilgrimage | | Solitary survivor | Care services | Example: Banks offer education loans to Full nest II families and pension plans to Empty nest I couples. Q35. Explain Maslow's hierarchy and Alderfer's ERG theory, with consumer applications. Maslow's five levels: Physiological needs concern food and basic survival; safety concerns protection and stability; belonging concerns affection and social connection; esteem concerns respect and achievement; self-actualisation concerns developing one's potential. A product can serve several needs: a phone can support communication, belonging and status. Draw the five-level pyramid shown in Q12. Limits: Needs may coexist, and culture and circumstances affect their importance. Do not assume every consumer follows an identical fixed sequence. Introduction Clayton Alderfer (1969) revised Maslow's theory to make it more flexible and closer to research evidence. He condensed Maslow's five needs into three groups – Existence, Relatedness and Growth (ERG). 1. The Three Needs 1. Existence needs (E): material and physiological needs (= Maslow's physiological + safety). 2. Relatedness needs (R): relationships with others (= social + external esteem). 3. Growth needs (G): personal development (= internal esteem + self-actualisation). ```mermaid flowchart LR M5["Self-actualisation"] --> G["GROWTH"] M4a["Esteem (internal)"] --> G M4b["Esteem (external)"] --> R["RELATEDNESS"] M3["Social"] --> R M2["Safety"] --> X["EXISTENCE"] M1["Physiological"] --> X ``` 2. Key Ideas of ERG Theory 1. More than one need can operate at the same time. 2. No rigid order of needs. 3. Satisfaction–progression: a satisfied need leads to the next one. 4. Frustration–regression: if a higher need is frustrated, a person falls back to a lower need with more intensity (a person unable to grow in career spends more on material comforts). Comparison Table | Basis | Maslow | Alderfer (ERG) | | --- | --- | --- | | Number of needs | 5 | 3 | | Order | Usually presented as a hierarchy | Flexible; simultaneous needs | | Needs at a time | One dominant need | Several together | | Movement | Satisfaction–progression only | Satisfaction–progression and frustration–regression | | Emphasis | Five need categories | Three categories and frustration–regression | Example: A young employee who cannot get a promotion (growth frustrated) may compensate by buying an expensive bike (existence). Q36. Explain Herzberg, McClelland and McGregor, and distinguish their applications. Introduction Frederick Herzberg (1959) studied what makes people satisfied or dissatisfied at work. He found that satisfaction and dissatisfaction are caused by two different sets of factors – hygiene factors and motivators. The same idea applies to how consumers judge products. 1. Hygiene Factors (Dissatisfiers / Maintenance Factors) Their absence causes dissatisfaction; their presence only prevents dissatisfaction. 1. Workplace: salary, job security, working conditions, company policy, supervision. 2. Consumer: warranty, basic quality, safety, on-time delivery. 2. Motivators (Satisfiers) Their presence causes satisfaction and motivation. 1. Workplace: achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth, the work itself. 2. Consumer: unique features, attractive design, delight factors, prestige. | Factor type | When absent | When present | | --- | --- | --- | | Hygiene factors | Dissatisfaction | No dissatisfaction (but not satisfaction) | | Motivators | No satisfaction (but not dissatisfaction) | Satisfaction | 3. Relevance to Consumer Behaviour 1. Marketers must first provide hygiene factors (reliability, after-sales service, safety) so consumers are not dissatisfied. 2. To create preference and loyalty, they must add motivators – innovative features, superior design, emotional benefits. Comparison Table | Basis | Hygiene factors | Motivators | | --- | --- | --- | | Effect when absent | Dissatisfaction | No satisfaction | | Effect when present | No dissatisfaction | Satisfaction | | Work examples | Salary, job security | Recognition, growth | | Car example | Airbags, service network | Panoramic sunroof, premium feel | Example: In a car, airbags and a good service network are hygiene factors; a panoramic sunroof and premium interiors are motivators. McClelland's acquired needs: Achievement is the desire to meet challenging standards and receive performance feedback; affiliation is the desire for belonging and harmonious relationships; power is the desire to influence others. Their relative importance differs across people and experiences. Marketing appeals can emphasise accomplishing goals, connecting with others or exercising influence, without assuming a purchase reveals a person's dominant motive. McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y: These are contrasting managerial assumptions about workers. X assumes work avoidance and a need for close direction; Y recognises that people can exercise self-direction, accept responsibility and be creative under suitable conditions. They are not scientifically established categories of shoppers. Use them to explain managerial attitudes, then label any consumer analogy as an analogy. Comparison: Herzberg distinguishes causes of workplace dissatisfaction and satisfaction; McClelland examines acquired needs; McGregor examines assumptions used in management. Herzberg's application to products is an extension of a workplace theory. Q37. Explain Vroom and the Porter–Lawler expectancy model with an example. Introduction Victor Vroom (1964) explained motivation as a rational calculation. A person is motivated when they believe effort will lead to performance, performance will lead to a reward, and the reward is valued. Formula: Motivation (Force) = Expectancy × Instrumentality × Valence ```mermaid flowchart LR E["EFFORT"] -- Expectancy --> P["PERFORMANCE"] -- Instrumentality --> R["REWARD"] -- Valence --> V["Value to the person"] ``` 1. Components 1. Expectancy (E): belief that effort will lead to performance (0 to 1). 2. Instrumentality (I): belief that performance will lead to the reward (0 to 1). 3. Valence (V): value or attractiveness of the reward to the person (−1 to +1). 4. Because motivation is a product, if any one factor is zero, motivation is zero. 2. Numerical Example Given: A consumer is considering a fitness programme. E = 0.7 (she believes she can follow it), I = 0.9 (she believes following it will reduce weight), V = 0.8 (she values weight loss highly). To find: Motivation (M). Formula: M = E × I × V Solution: M = 0.7 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.504 Answer: Motivation = 0.504. Interpretation: an illustrative motivation score, not a purchase probability. If she believed the programme would give no results (I = 0), motivation would be 0. 3. Consumer Relevance 1. Increase expectancy – "easy to use", simple instructions. 2. Increase instrumentality – guarantees, proof, testimonials, cashback. 3. Increase valence – attractive rewards and emotional benefits. Comparison Table | Component | Question in the consumer's mind | Marketer's tool | | --- | --- | --- | | Expectancy | "Can I do it?" | Easy-to-use claims, demos | | Instrumentality | "Will it give the result?" | Guarantees, testimonials | | Valence | "Do I want the result?" | Attractive benefits | Porter–Lawler model: The value of a reward and perceived effort–reward probability influence effort. Performance depends on effort together with abilities, traits and understanding of the role. Performance produces intrinsic rewards, such as achievement, and extrinsic rewards, such as a prize. Satisfaction depends on the rewards and whether they seem equitable; experience affects future expectations. Flow: reward value + perceived probability → effort → performance (also influenced by ability and role clarity) → intrinsic/extrinsic rewards → perceived fairness → satisfaction and feedback. Difference: Vroom explains the motivation to exert effort; Porter–Lawler links effort, performance, rewards and satisfaction. For a loyalty scheme, consumers must value the reward, understand how to earn it and receive a reward they perceive as fair. Q38. Explain Freud's theory of motivation and its use in consumer research. Introduction Sigmund Freud believed that human behaviour is driven largely by unconscious motives – desires people are not aware of. Applied to marketing, this means consumers may not know the real reasons why they buy. 1. Structure of Personality 1. Id: primitive, unconscious urges seeking immediate pleasure (pleasure principle). 2. Superego: the internal moral conscience – social and family values. 3. Ego: the conscious controller that balances the id and superego realistically (reality principle). ```mermaid flowchart TD SE["SUPEREGO
'Don't overspend, it's wrong'"] --> EG["EGO
balances → 'Buy it on a sale'"] ID["ID
'I want that luxury watch now!'"] --> EG ``` 2. Motivation Research Ernest Dichter applied Freud's ideas to marketing using qualitative techniques to uncover hidden motives: 1. Depth interviews: long, unstructured one-to-one interviews. 2. Focus groups: group discussions. 3. Projective techniques: word association, sentence completion, picture interpretation (TAT), role playing. 3. Marketing Implications 1. Use of symbolic and emotional appeals. 2. Products seen as extensions of personality. 3. Luxury purchases explained as satisfying hidden status or pleasure motives. 4. Guilt-reduction messages ("you deserve it"). Advantages: - Reveals hidden reasons for buying. - Helps create emotional and symbolic advertising. Limitations: - Based on small samples. - Interpretation is subjective. - Hard to measure or test scientifically. Comparison Table | Part | Principle | Consumer voice | | --- | --- | --- | | Id | Pleasure | "I want it now!" | | Superego | Morality | "It's wasteful." | | Ego | Reality | "Buy it on sale." | Example: A chocolate ad says "Go on, treat yourself – you deserve it", satisfying the id while calming the superego. Q39. Explain self-concept, trait, humanistic and social-cognitive personality theories. Introduction Unlike Freudian theory, which is qualitative, trait theory is a quantitative approach. It describes personality in terms of measurable traits – distinguishing, relatively enduring ways in which one person differs from another (such as sociable, confident or anxious). 1. Main Trait Theorists 1. Gordon Allport: cardinal, central and secondary traits. 2. Raymond Cattell: 16 personality factors (16PF), measured by questionnaire. 3. Big Five (OCEAN) model: five broad traits that describe most personalities. 2. The Big Five (OCEAN) Traits 1. Openness: curious, creative – tries new products, travel, gadgets. 2. Conscientiousness: organised, careful – compares carefully, values reliability. 3. Extraversion: sociable, outgoing – enjoys social events, fashion, group activities. 4. Agreeableness: friendly, cooperative – influenced by others' opinions. 5. Neuroticism: anxious, emotionally unstable – seeks reassurance, comfort and safety products. 3. Consumer-Specific Traits 1. Consumer innovativeness: willingness to try new products. 2. Dogmatism: rigidity towards unfamiliar ideas. 3. Social character: inner-directed vs other-directed. 4. Need for uniqueness and variety-seeking. 5. Optimum stimulation level and need for cognition. 6. Materialism and compulsive buying. 7. Consumer ethnocentrism: preference for domestic products ("Vocal for Local"). Advantages: - Measurable with questionnaires. - Useful for market segmentation. Limitations: - Traits alone poorly predict specific brand choice. - The situation also influences behaviour. Comparison Table | Trait | High scorers are | Consumer example | | --- | --- | --- | | Openness | Curious, creative | Try new gadgets | | Conscientiousness | Organised, careful | Read reviews, value reliability | | Extraversion | Sociable | Fashion, group activities | | Agreeableness | Cooperative | Follow friends' advice | | Neuroticism | Anxious | Buy safety and comfort products | Example: Consumers high in openness are the first to buy new tech such as foldable phones. Memory aid: OCEAN. Self-concept: Actual self is how someone sees themselves; ideal self is how they would like to be; social self is how they believe others see them; ideal social self is how they would like others to see them. Products may express or support these identities. For example, buying running shoes may support an aspiration to be more active; it does not prove the buyer already has that lifestyle. Humanistic theory: Maslow and Rogers emphasise growth, choice and personal potential. Rogers discusses self-concept and congruence between self and experience. Consumer applications include services that support learning and personal development, rather than assuming material purchases automatically produce fulfilment. Social-cognitive theory: Personal beliefs, behaviour and environment influence one another (reciprocal determinism). People learn from models and from consequences; self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to perform a specific task. Product demonstrations can build confidence. Unlike a trait-only explanation, this approach emphasises both the person and the situation. Comparison: Self-concept asks how buying relates to identity; trait theory measures individual differences; humanistic theory emphasises development; social-cognitive theory examines interaction and learning. Psychoanalytic and Neo-Freudian approaches remain in Q14. Q40. Explain operant, associative, trial-and-error and social learning with examples. Introduction Operant conditioning, developed by B. F. Skinner, is learning based on the consequences of behaviour. Behaviour that is rewarded (reinforced) is likely to be repeated; behaviour that is punished or not rewarded is less likely. The consumer learns by trial and error which behaviours give the best results. Skinner box experiment: a rat that pressed a lever received food, so it learned to press the lever more often. ```mermaid flowchart LR B["Behaviour
(buy brand)"] --> C["Consequence"] --> R{"Reinforced?"} R -- Yes --> Y["Repeat purchase"] R -- No --> N["Stop buying"] ``` 1. Types of Reinforcement 1. Positive reinforcement: a pleasant reward after behaviour – the product works well; cashback, loyalty points. 2. Negative reinforcement: removing an unpleasant state – a painkiller removes a headache; insurance removes fear. 3. Punishment: an unpleasant result reduces behaviour – late payment fees. 4. Extinction: behaviour fades when the reward stops – a customer leaves when satisfaction ends. 2. Schedules of Reinforcement 1. Total (continuous): every purchase is rewarded (free gift every time). 2. Systematic (fixed ratio): every nth purchase is rewarded ("buy 9 coffees, get the 10th free"). 3. Random (variable ratio): rewards given at random (lucky draws, scratch cards). 3. Other Applications 1. Shaping: rewarding small steps towards the desired behaviour (free test drive → showroom visit → purchase). 2. Massed vs distributed learning: a concentrated ad burst gives quick learning (product launch); spread-out ads give longer-lasting learning. Comparison Table (Classical vs Operant) | Basis | Classical conditioning | Operant conditioning | | --- | --- | --- | | Proposed by | Pavlov | Skinner | | Learning through | Association of stimuli | Consequences (rewards / punishment) | | Response | Involuntary (automatic) | Voluntary | | Consumer role | Passive | Active | | Example | Jingle linked with brand | Cashback after purchase | Example: A coffee chain's app gives a free coffee after every nine purchases, encouraging customers to keep coming back (fixed-ratio positive reinforcement). Associative and trial-and-error learning: Consumers learn links between cues and outcomes and retain these in memory. In trial-and-error learning, they try alternatives and adjust later choices according to consequences. Thorndike's law of effect explains why a response followed by a satisfying result tends to be strengthened. A successful trial pack can encourage repurchase, but a poor experience can discourage it. Social/observational learning: Attention to a model → retention of the demonstrated behaviour → ability to reproduce it → motivation to do so. A customer can learn to use an appliance by watching a demonstration without first receiving a direct reward. Credible, relatable models and clear demonstrations aid learning. Distinguish the mechanisms: Classical conditioning links stimuli; operant conditioning links behaviour with consequences; observational learning involves watching others; cognitive approaches also examine expectations and understanding. These mechanisms can operate together. Q41. Explain the cognitive theories of learning: social cognitive theory, cognitive behavioural theory and constructivism. Introduction Cognitive learning views the consumer as an active problem-solver who learns through mental processes – thinking, information processing and reasoning – rather than only through reward and repetition. Three important cognitive theories are social cognitive theory, cognitive behavioural theory and constructivism. 1. Social Cognitive Theory (Albert Bandura) Learning results from the interaction of personal factors (beliefs, expectations), behaviour and environment – reciprocal determinism. 1. Self-efficacy: belief in one's ability to perform a behaviour decides whether a person tries it. 2. Observational learning from models. 3. Marketing use: tutorials, "easy to use" claims, success stories that build confidence. Example: A woman believes she can cook well with a smart kitchen appliance after watching tutorials, so she buys it. 2. Cognitive Behavioural Theory (Aaron Beck) Our thoughts (cognitions) influence our feelings and behaviour; changing thoughts can change behaviour. ```mermaid flowchart LR T["THOUGHTS"] --- F["FEELINGS"] --- B["BEHAVIOUR"] ``` 1. A thought ("I deserve a reward") creates a feeling (excitement), which leads to behaviour (an impulse purchase). 2. Reframing thoughts ("Do I need this?") reduces impulse buying. 3. Marketing / social use: campaigns that change beliefs to change behaviour (anti-smoking, saving money, healthy eating). Example: A savings app asks users "Will you still want this in a week?" before an online purchase, reducing impulse spending. 3. Constructivism (Jean Piaget, Lev Vygotsky) Learners actively construct their own knowledge by linking new information with existing knowledge and experience. 1. Piaget: learning through assimilation (fitting new information into existing ideas) and accommodation (changing ideas to fit new information). 2. Vygotsky: learning is social – it happens through interaction and guidance from others. 3. Marketing use: interactive demos, experiential marketing, product trials, online communities and comparison tools. Example: A first-time investor understands mutual funds by exploring apps, comparing them with bank FDs and discussing them with friends. 4. Supporting Ideas 1. Information processing: consumers receive information, store it in memory (sensory → short-term → long-term) and retrieve it when deciding. 2. Involvement theory: high-involvement purchases get deep processing; low-involvement purchases get little. Comparison Table | Theory | Proposed by | Key idea | Marketing use | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Social cognitive | Bandura | Person–behaviour–environment interaction; self-efficacy | Tutorials, success stories | | Cognitive behavioural | Beck | Thoughts drive feelings and behaviour | Belief-change campaigns | | Constructivism | Piaget, Vygotsky | Learners build their own knowledge | Demos, trials, communities | Q42. What are evaluative criteria and decision rules? Explain with examples. Introduction While choosing between brands, consumers compare them on certain features and then follow a rule to decide. Evaluative criteria are the product features or attributes used to compare alternatives – for example price, brand, quality, battery life and after-sales service. Decision rules (heuristics) are the procedures consumers use to choose among alternatives. 1. Compensatory Rule A weakness on one attribute can be compensated by strength on another. The brand with the highest total weighted score is chosen. Example – choosing a phone: | Attribute (weight) | Brand A | Brand B | | --- | --- | --- | | Camera (0.5) | 8 | 6 | | Battery (0.3) | 5 | 9 | | Price (0.2) | 6 | 8 | | Weighted score | 8×0.5 + 5×0.3 + 6×0.2 = 6.7 | 6×0.5 + 9×0.3 + 8×0.2 = 7.3 | Brand B is chosen (7.3 > 6.7) although Brand A has the better camera. 2. Non-Compensatory Rules A weakness cannot be made up by other strengths. 1. Conjunctive rule: set a minimum cut-off for every attribute; reject any brand below a cut-off. (Battery must be at least 6 → Brand A rejected.) 2. Disjunctive rule: set a high cut-off on one or a few key attributes; accept any brand that exceeds it. (Camera at least 8 → Brand A accepted.) 3. Lexicographic rule: rank attributes by importance and choose the brand best on the most important attribute. (Camera most important → Brand A.) 3. Affect Referral Rule Choose the brand with the best overall feeling or attitude, without detailed evaluation ("I always trust Tata"). Comparison Table | Rule | Type | How the choice is made | Result in example | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Compensatory | Compensatory | Highest weighted score | Brand B | | Conjunctive | Non-compensatory | Minimum on all attributes | Brand B | | Disjunctive | Non-compensatory | High on key attribute | Brand A | | Lexicographic | Non-compensatory | Best on most important | Brand A | | Affect referral | Simplified | Overall liking | Favourite brand | Memory aid: C-C-D-L-A – Compensatory, Conjunctive, Disjunctive, Lexicographic, Affect referral. Q43. Explain the Sheth model of industrial buyer behaviour. Introduction In industrial buying, decisions are often made jointly by people from different departments who may disagree. The Sheth model (Jagdish Sheth, 1973) explains this joint decision making in industrial (organisational) buying through four main elements. Diagram: ```mermaid flowchart TD A["1. Psychological world of decision makers → EXPECTATIONS
background, information sources, active search,
perceptual distortion, satisfaction with past purchases"] B["2. Product- and company-specific factors → AUTONOMOUS or JOINT decision
time pressure, perceived risk, type of purchase;
orientation, size, centralisation"] C["3. Conflict resolution
problem solving, persuasion, bargaining, politicking"] D["4. Situational factors → SUPPLIER / BRAND CHOICE
strikes, recession, price changes, natural disasters"] A --> B --> C --> D ``` 1. Psychological World of the Decision Makers 1. Purchasing agents, engineers, users and others have different expectations about suppliers and brands. 2. Expectations depend on background (education, role orientation, lifestyle), information sources (salespeople, exhibitions, journals), active search, perceptual distortion and satisfaction with past purchases. 2. Factors Deciding Autonomous vs Joint Decisions 1. Product-specific factors: time pressure (urgent → autonomous), perceived risk (high → joint), type of purchase (new or capital item → joint; routine → autonomous). 2. Company-specific factors: company orientation (technology- or production-oriented), company size (large → joint), degree of centralisation (decentralised → joint decisions more likely). 3. Conflict Resolution in Joint Decisions 1. Problem solving: gathering more information and deliberating – rational. 2. Persuasion: convincing others that one's criteria fit company goals. 3. Bargaining: give-and-take ("you choose this time, I choose next time"). 4. Politicking: using power and tactics – least rational and may harm the organisation. 4. Situational Factors Unexpected events – strikes, recession, price controls, supplier problems, natural calamities – may override the planned choice. Advantages: - Recognises group decisions and conflict. - Useful for B2B selling. Limitations: - Complex and hard to measure. - Less focus on post-purchase behaviour. Comparison Table (conflict resolution methods) | Method | Nature | Rationality | | --- | --- | --- | | Problem solving | More information, discussion | Most rational | | Persuasion | Convincing others | Rational | | Bargaining | Give-and-take | Less rational | | Politicking | Power and tactics | Least rational | Example: When a factory buys a new machine, engineers prefer quality and the finance team prefers low cost; they resolve the conflict by gathering more supplier data (problem solving). Q44. Explain the types of communication systems: interpersonal, impersonal and persuasive communication. Introduction Marketers reach consumers in different ways – through a salesperson's conversation, a TV ad or a carefully designed persuasive campaign. Communication systems are classified as interpersonal, impersonal and persuasive communication. 1. Interpersonal Communication Direct, face-to-face or personal communication between two or more people. 1. Can be formal (salesperson to customer) or informal (word of mouth among friends and family). 2. Two-way, with immediate feedback; highly persuasive and trusted. 3. Examples: personal selling, word of mouth, opinion leaders, phone calls, WhatsApp recommendations. 2. Impersonal Communication Communication directed at a large, anonymous audience through mass media. 1. One-way, with delayed and indirect feedback (sales, surveys). 2. Examples: TV, radio, newspaper and magazine ads, billboards, websites, social media posts, public relations. 3. Persuasive Communication Communication intended to change attitudes or behaviour – to make consumers buy, try or prefer a brand. Factors that make communication persuasive: 1. Source credibility: expertise, trustworthiness and attractiveness of the source (doctors for toothpaste, celebrities). 2. Message structure: one-sided (only benefits – for favourable audiences) vs two-sided (benefits and limitations – more credible for educated audiences); order effects (primacy and recency); repetition. 3. Message appeals: - Rational appeal: facts, features, price, performance. - Emotional appeals: fear (insurance, road safety), humour, love, nostalgia, pride, guilt. - Comparative advertising: comparison with competitors. - Attractiveness appeal: used carefully. 4. Audience characteristics: involvement, knowledge, personality. Persuasion models: AIDA – Attention → Interest → Desire → Action; Hierarchy of effects – awareness → knowledge → liking → preference → conviction → purchase. Comparison Table | Basis | Interpersonal | Impersonal | | --- | --- | --- | | Audience | Individual or small group | Large mass audience | | Direction | Two-way | Mostly one-way | | Feedback | Immediate | Delayed | | Cost per person | High | Low | | Trust | High | Lower | | Example | Salesperson, word of mouth | TV ad, billboard | Example: A car company runs TV ads (impersonal), trains showroom staff (interpersonal) and uses a fear appeal about road safety to promote airbags (persuasive).
